sentence: There are millions of people in this world who think exactly like you.
People who feel too much, who think too deep, who've spent their whole life feeling like an alien.
And I want you to understand something uncomfortable: you've probably walked past three of them this week.

sentence: At the store.
At work.
On the street.
And you didn't recognize each other.
Not because you're bad at noticing.
But because both of you were hiding.
Here's the strangest irony of being a rare personality type.
You spend your life desperate to find people who understand you.
And yet, you've become an expert at making sure nobody can see you.
Let me show you what I mean.
There's a loneliness that isn't about being alone.
You can be surrounded by people — a party, a family dinner, an office — and still feel like you're watching everyone through glass.

sentence: You can have friends and still feel unknown.
That's the loneliness of the deep.
It's not that nobody's around.
It's that nobody's really there.
And the worst part?
The conversations that are supposed to connect you — the small talk, the pleasantries, the "how was your weekend" — they don't fill the loneliness.
They sharpen it.

sentence: Because you leave those conversations feeling more alone than when you started.
You wanted depth, and you got weather.
So you keep searching.
And here's where it gets painful.
Every rare type is searching for the same thing.
But every rare type is also hiding behind a costume.
The INFJ wears the social mask.

sentence: They mirror whoever they're with, so smoothly that the person across from them only ever sees a reflection of themselves.
Nobody meets the real INFJ, because the real INFJ was trained to disappear.

sentence: They'll show you their work, their ideas, their plans — anything but their inner world.
You can work next to an INTJ for years and never once meet the person inside.

sentence: They'll hand you a poem, a song, a dream — a beautiful, safe stand-in for themselves.
It's easier to show you their creation than their face.

sentence: A joke for every feeling.
A deflection for every real question.
They've learned that being sincere costs too much.
And here's the tragedy.
You're all standing in the same room, in different costumes, looking for each other.

sentence: Carl Jung understood this better than anyone.
He said that becoming who you truly are — individuation — is the loneliest journey a human can take.

sentence: Because the more you become yourself, the less you belong to the crowd.

sentence: So how do you find each other?

sentence: You don't have to be the mirror, the achiever, the artist, or the joker.

sentence: Rare types don't gather at small-talk parties.

sentence: They ask why, not what.
They go quiet before they speak deeply.
They light up when the conversation goes somewhere real.
When you see it, don't let it pass.
Because here's the truth I need you to hold onto.
The loneliness you feel isn't proof that you're unlovable.
It's proof that you've been looking for your people in a crowd that was never yours.
